claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by formation of a dense, adherent oxide film.
High-temperature processing causes preferential surface segregation of oxide-forming elements such as Al, Cr, or Ti.
The segregated elements form a dense and adherent protective oxide during processing.
A dense oxide film minimizes chemical attack by a corrosive medium.
A dense oxide film minimizes mechanical removal of the alloy substrate.
The initial material can be a nanocrystalline or spark-plasma-sintered HEA with a BCC or multiphase solid-solution structure.
The initial material lacks a preformed protective oxide scale.
Higher-temperature sintering or controlled oxidation promotes surface enrichment and formation of a dense, continuous, spinel-type oxide film.
The oxide film lowers the electrochemically active corrosion area by limiting ion diffusion.
The oxide film is a sacrificial and mechanically compliant barrier that reduces direct metal-to-counterbody contact.
Formation of the oxide film makes corrosion diffusion-controlled and lowers corrosion current density.
The oxide film lowers wear rate by preventing abrasion-driven substrate loss.
Oxide-film-forming processing will produce lower corrosion current density than processing that does not promote the film.
Oxide-film-forming processing will produce lower wear depth than a matched baseline lacking the film.
Simultaneous reductions in chemical attack and mechanical degradation will lower total degradation under combined wear-corrosion testing.
Lower sintering temperature or reduced oxygen exposure produces a porous or discontinuous surface film.
The protective effect should persist when the oxide is stable and adherent, oxygen is available, and mechanical stresses are moderate.
The protection may fail when wear removes the film faster than it reforms or when oxygen availability is insufficient for film formation.
